content: The Data Quality Review (DQR) framework evaluates several critical dimensions of data quality in health systems: 1. Completeness and Timeliness: This dimension assesses whether the data reported through the system is both complete and submitted on time, ensuring accurate calculation of health indicators. 2. Internal Consistency of Reported Data: This involves evaluating the plausibility of reported data by comparing it with historical values of the same indicators or expected relationships between indicators. It also includes verifying the accuracy of reported data against source documents at health facilities. 3. External Consistency with Other Data Sources: 4. External Comparisons of Population Data: This examines the adequacy of population data used in calculating health indicator denominators, such as rates or proportions. To improve data quality and reduce the reporting burden on healthcare professionals and administrative staff, it is essential to design effective data collection tools and forms. Analyzing data from these tools and generating outputs that help managers and stakeholders identify problems and areas of focus is a key aspect of routine data review and decision-making. This guideline encourages managers to regularly review data across the HIV services cascade, supplemented periodically with data from models, surveys, and special studies to validate program performance assessments, including impact evaluations. Routine data reviews should prioritize a simple set of selected indicators based on recommended minimum datasets, which can be analyzed at national, subnational, and facility levels. National program managers should conduct these reviews at least annually, ideally more frequently, focusing on geographic divisions (e.g., subnational, facility) and disaggregated data by age, gender, and key populations to highlight disparities in service access and quality. Subnational managers (e.g., provincial or district levels) may conduct quarterly reviews, while facility managers may review data even more frequently to monitor progress and support staff in delivering services efficiently and effectively. In addition to routine program data, regular evaluations and operational research are necessary to address complex questions, test new service delivery approaches, and learn from implementation. These efforts complement routine data reviews as part of a data-driven approach to continuous quality improvement and service coverage. Limited resources necessitate focusing investments on programs and services that are appropriate, well-implemented, effective, and efficient. Establishing and updating a regular evaluation agenda helps countries prioritize key program areas and address critical bottlenecks in implementation. Research and evaluation studies should be planned and managed as discrete projects with formal processes and oversight. The evaluation agenda should consider the feasibility of using existing data to focus on filling gaps rather than duplicating efforts. Sound design and management of evaluations and operational research require technical expertise tailored to the specific needs of the country and program context. Individual-level data is often better suited for addressing research questions than aggregate data. Disaggregated data is essential for assessing equity and performance in health service access and outcomes among different geographic, sociodemographic, and patient subgroups. Routine equity assessments in service delivery and quality are fundamental to honoring the commitment to equity in the HIV response. Identifying and addressing gaps in underserved groups is the fastest way to achieve overall program targets. Disaggregation categories include geography (e.g., cities, regions, districts, facilities), age, gender (male, female, transgender, and gender-diverse), and key populations (e.g., men who have sex with men, people in prisons, people who inject drugs, sex workers, transgender individuals). Consistency in disaggregation categories across indicators is critical for effective analysis and accurate data recording. Age disaggregation helps identify service quality and uptake bottlenecks affecting children and adolescents differently from adults, as well as age-specific barriers to health-seeking behavior or adherence. Narrower age bands are recommended in settings with robust electronic health information systems. For example, indicators specific to vertical transmission use narrower age bands, such as 0–2 months and 2–12 months for early infant diagnosis, or up to 24 months for ARV coverage during breastfeeding. Gender disaggregation includes male, female, and other categories, with the latter encompassing transgender and gender-diverse individuals. Key population data should be collected and analyzed where feasible and safe, ensuring data security and confidentiality. Key population status should not be recorded in patient monitoring tools containing personally identifiable information. Instead, it may be recorded anonymously or in a non-identifying manner for prevention or testing services. Geographic disaggregation enables managers to focus services more effectively and identify underserved communities. Disseminating geographically disaggregated data through maps requires precautions to protect confidentiality, especially in areas with small populations or high stigma and discrimination. The collection of person-centered data allows tracking of service uptake over time, such as whether a second viral load test was conducted within six months of an initial high result or whether HIV-exposed infants received virological testing within two months of birth. Aggregate data collection for such indicators may require specialized tools or digital systems capable of tracking individual patients over time. Community-based service data is increasingly important for effective program monitoring and management. Data systems must integrate information from community-based services, such as mobile clinics or outreach workers, while avoiding double counting of individuals referred between community and facility-based services. Community engagement is essential for linking these data systems effectively. For example, the total number of condoms distributed during a reporting period is an important indicator of proactive distribution strategies. Data on condom distribution can be disaggregated by type (male or female), distribution modality (commercial, social marketing, public sector), and provider type (e.g., key population-led organizations, public sector providers). PrEP data can be disaggregated by gender, age, key populations, PrEP product type, and service setting (facility-based or community-based). In summary, robust data collection, disaggregation, and analysis are critical for improving equity, service quality, and program performance in HIV prevention, care, and treatment.
